blocks.label: IP and port: identifying a machine and a service
blocks.text: An IP address identifies the destination machine or network interface on a network. An IP address alone does not determine which service on that machine the traffic should reach.

blocks.label: A port is a number that distinguishes services communicating over the same IP address. Clients connect to a combination of an IP address and a port, such as port 443, where a web server receives HTTPS traffic.
blocks.text: When a connection cannot be made, check separately whether the name resolves to an IP address, whether there is a route to that IP address, and whether access to the destination port is allowed and a service is listening on it. Knowing the IP address alone does not guarantee that the application can be reached.

blocks.label: TCP and UDP: Connection and Delivery Characteristics
blocks.text: TCP is a transport protocol that establishes a connection and handles ordering and delivery. It is used when you need to detect lost data and handle it in the correct order, as with web communications.

blocks.label: UDP sends datagrams and does not provide connection establishment, retransmission, or ordering control as part of the protocol, unlike TCP. For use cases that prioritize low latency, consider at the application level which controls are needed.
blocks.text: Do not choose based only on the idea that “TCP is slow and UDP is fast.” Check where ordering, retransmission, and connection management are handled, as well as the characteristics the use case requires.

blocks.label: HTTP and TLS: The meaning of requests and protection of the communication channel
blocks.text: HTTP is an application protocol that lets clients and servers exchange requests and responses. Methods such as GET and POST, along with status codes, are part of HTTP’s meaning.

blocks.label: TLS is a protocol that provides authentication of communicating parties, confidentiality, and integrity. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS; it does not itself define the meaning of HTTP URLs or responses.
blocks.text: When troubleshooting a failure, check in order whether the TCP connection is established, whether the TLS handshake succeeds, and whether an HTTP response is returned. Do not treat a certificate problem at the same stage as an HTTP 404.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting: Work through each layer from the outside in
blocks.text: If you call every connectivity problem a “network outage,” you can’t narrow down the cause. Check each layer in order: the name the user entered, the DNS result, the IP route, port permissions such as those in a security group, TCP/UDP, TLS, and the HTTP response.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting: Work through each layer from the outside in
blocks.text: Establish what you observe at each layer. If DNS can’t resolve a name to an IP address, it’s too early to investigate ports or HTTP. If a TCP connection is refused, the request hasn’t reached the HTTP application.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting: Work through each layer from the outside in
blocks.text: Match each change to a hypothesis about the cause. Before broadening port permissions, confirm that the destination and port are required and that the service is listening. After making a fix, repeat the observation at the same layer.
